target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and increase voting access
objection: A federal holiday designation would not, by itself, require private employers to close or give paid time off, so many workers—especially in private-sector retail and service jobs—would still face the same work-schedule barriers.

target: AG1's assumption that the holiday would help everyone equally
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately in hourly retail, service, and other inflexible jobs, and they are less able to take unpaid time off without losing wages or risking job consequences, so the holiday would especially fail to help them.

target: AG1's conclusion that a national holiday would be an equitable voting-access reform
objection: If scheduling barriers remain for many low-income workers, the holiday would likely disadvantage them relative to higher-resourced voters who can more easily adjust to Election Day timing.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday is a strong turnout reform
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1's overall policy recommendation
objection: A policy that does not reliably address low-income voters’ constraints and is not an effective turnout lever is not a good voting-access strategy; more targeted reforms such as employer time-off requirements and automatic voter registration are better.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday would not reliably remove work-schedule barriers
objection: A national-holiday policy can be written to require employer time off for voting, so it need not be merely a symbolic calendar label; paired with time-off obligations, it would reduce barriers even for private-sector workers.

target: AG2's claim that the policy would disadvantage low-income workers
objection: If the holiday guarantees time to vote during the workday, it particularly helps hourly low-income workers who have the least flexibility and are most constrained by wage and schedule tradeoffs.

target: AG2's equity critique that the holiday fails low-income voters
objection: A properly implemented Election Day holiday with guaranteed voting time would improve access for low-income workers rather than disadvantaging them.

target: AG2's recommendation to prioritize state-only reforms instead of a holiday
objection: The appropriate response to scheduling barriers is a reliable federal measure that removes those barriers; a national holiday paired with time-off requirements can do that.

target: AG2's repeated claim that private employers would likely stay open and leave workers without time off
objection: Many workplaces reduce hours or close on federal holidays, so a national Election Day holiday would in practice give many employees more time away from work to vote, even if some workplaces remain open.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would not help families because school schedules still constrain them
objection: School and daycare closures or reduced operations on a federal holiday would reduce childcare barriers and give parents more opportunity to vote.

target: AG2's conclusion that the holiday would not help low-income workers relative to higher-resourced voters
objection: By reducing work and school-related constraints, a holiday addresses the key barriers faced by low-income families and therefore is not likely to disadvantage them relative to higher-resourced voters.

target: AG2's claim that weekend/holiday election timing in other OECD countries is irrelevant or unsupported
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that shifting election timing is feasible in established democracies and can be built into national civic routines.

target: AG2's implication that broad support does not matter because implementation might be symbolic
objection: Cross-party support makes the policy politically feasible and increases the chance it would be implemented with practical details that address the real barriers voters care about, rather than being purely symbolic.

target: AG2's argument that pre-Election Day voting means an Election Day holiday is unnecessary
objection: Because most jurisdictions offer early in-person or mail/absentee voting over a broader period, a holiday can still help by giving constrained workers more accessible days to use those options, reducing overall work-schedule barriers.

target: AG2's claim that pre-Election Day options still leave low-income workers constrained, so the holiday hurts them
objection: Low-income workers are more likely to have inflexible hourly jobs, but a holiday can give them extra accessible days to vote through early or mail/absentee options, so it is more likely to help than harm them.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would also solve registration and ballot-access prerequisites
objection: Voting depends not only on time to vote, but also on registration status and ballot-deadline compliance; a holiday changes the calendar but does not automatically fix those bottlenecks.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would improve access for low-income voters on registration and ballot-access issues
objection: Low-income voters face more friction in administrative steps like documentation and deadline compliance, and a holiday does not directly address those hurdles.

target: AG1's suggestion that time off on Election Day is the best primary reform
objection: Targeted reforms such as state employer-time-off laws and automatic voter registration directly address time-to-vote and registration-readiness problems more effectively than a calendar holiday.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday does not help registration and ballot-access because many deadlines occur before Election Day
objection: Many registration and ballot-access tasks are time-sensitive administrative steps that overlap work or school hours, so protected time away from work or school can still help people complete them and meet deadlines.

target: AG2's argument that low-income voters would still be stuck with bottlenecks
objection: If the holiday increases the time available to finish prerequisite steps, it directly helps low-income workers who cannot easily take normal business hours off to handle paperwork and deadlines.

target: AG1's claim that a single Election Day holiday can clear registration and ballot-access bottlenecks
objection: Many prerequisites depend on deadlines before Election Day and on documents or records that take more than one day to obtain or verify, so extra time on Election Day does not reliably remove those barriers.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday fixes administrative access problems
objection: Some ballot-access steps require staffed government offices or service providers during normal business hours, and a federal holiday does not necessarily keep those offices open or speed processing.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would help low-income voters proportionally
objection: Low-income voters are less likely to have readily available documentation or the resources to rapidly obtain it, so one protected day helps them less than better-resourced voters.

target: AG1's broader claim that the holiday is a reliable registration/ballot-access fix
objection: Automatic voter registration and employer time-off requirements address registration-status and time-to-vote problems more directly than a one-day holiday, so the holiday should not be treated as a reliable solution.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday meaningfully helps with voter-controlled prerequisite steps
objection: Many bottlenecks depend on receipt and processing by election officials or supporting systems, and a holiday may even delay those processes rather than solve them.

target: AG1's claim that holiday time is enough to complete registration or ballot steps
objection: If receipt and processing depend on office schedules and mail systems, a single day of protected time does not reliably eliminate the bottleneck across voters and jurisdictions.

target: AG1's claim that holiday closures and reduced hours create usable time for low-income parents and workers
objection: Holiday closures do not automatically give low-income workers or parents usable time, because many still must work and cannot afford alternative childcare, so the scheduling benefit is not reliable.

target: AG1's claim that holiday-based time off is a reliable way to reduce registration and ballot-access bottlenecks for low-income voters
objection: If low-income voters cannot actually use the holiday time to complete the needed steps, then a federal Election Day holiday is not a reliable access measure for those bottlenecks.

target: AG2's claim that only one-day protected time is irrelevant because many bottlenecks are driven by outside processing
objection: A key driver of registration and ballot-access bottlenecks is voters’ own time-sensitive tasks—like gathering documents, filling forms, and attending appointments—that overlap work and school hours, so protected time can materially reduce those barriers even if processing speed does not change.

target: AG2's claim that record-availability problems make the holiday ineffective
objection: Some bottlenecks depend on steps that voters themselves must complete during deadlines, and extra protected time can help them finish those tasks even if outside record processing still takes time.

target: AG2's claim that processing delays around the holiday would cancel out any benefit
objection: Many deadlines and resolution windows occur on or near Election Day, so time off during that period can help voters complete cure, request, and submission steps on time despite administrative schedules.

target: AG2's claim that holiday time does not reliably help low-income voters complete administrative tasks
objection: Federal holidays often reduce hours or close many schools and workplaces, which increases time off and makes it more likely that low-income hourly workers can complete voter-controlled registration and ballot-access steps.

target: AG2's claim that holiday closures do not translate into usable time for parents or workers
objection: Because many schools and nonessential workplaces reduce hours or close on federal holidays, a federal Election Day holiday would realistically create additional protected time for many workers and parents to handle voting-related tasks.

target: AG2's broader argument that the holiday is unreliable for low-income voters because they may still work
objection: A national holiday can materially reduce the binding schedule constraints faced by low-income hourly workers, so it is a reliable way to help them clear registration and ballot-access prerequisites.
